spans.assertion: fitted a mixed effects logistic regression with crossed random effects for referees and players to test whether referees give more red cards to darker skin-toned players
the crossed random effects specification is claimed to generalize results beyond the sampled referees/players and to account for the data's correlational structure from clustering

found that players with darker skin tone receive more red cards over their career than lighter skin-toned players, controlling for position and league country, ORlightest,darkest = 1.382 [1.120, 1.705]

concludes the reasons for the increased red cards given to darker skin-toned players remain ambiguous

spans.assertion: included all player-referee dyads for 2,052 players in the first male divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain (2012-13 season) and all 3,147 referees they played under, yielding 146,028 dyads
notes that multiple dyads could relate to the same players or referees
employed a generalized linear mixed effects logistic regression with crossed random effects for players and referees because of the dataset's correlational structure
restates that the crossed random effects specification generalizes results beyond the sample and accounts for correlational structure due to clustering
used R 3.0.1 and the lme4 package (1.1-7) for all analyses
made data and analysis scripts available at http://osf.io/w6pi5
set the alpha level at .05 and reported 95% confidence intervals throughout

spans.note: describes original data collection: skin tone assessed by two independent raters on a 5-point Likert scale

spans.assertion: found inter-rater agreement for skin tone ratings was high, ICCavg = .955 [.951, .959], F(1584,1585) = 22.30, p < .001
used the mean of the two raters' skin tone ratings as the predictor in the analyses

collapsed the position variable's levels into Back, Middle, and Front because position was recorded only at the time of data extraction and players are unlikely to move into a defensive position over their career
used dummy coding for player position and league country with Back and England as reference categories
treated skin tone ratings and referee-home-country racial prejudice measures as predictors of interest, and wanted to include player position as a covariate
excluded cases missing skin tone ratings, referee-country prejudice data, or player position data (n = 30,014, 20.55%), assuming data were missing completely at random
excluded dyads involving referees who in total encountered only one player (n = 513, 0.35%)
lme4's default Nelder-Mead optimization did not converge on the full dataset
the initial-approach analytic sample consisted of 115,501 dyads
using non-collapsed positions in the final approach yielded a similar effect size estimate, ORlightest,darkest = 1.371 [1.101, 1.709]

spans.assertion: found that in most dyads no red cards were given, and no dyad had more than two red cards
considered the binomial distribution as an alternative to the Poisson distribution given the sparse count data and the known number of games per dyad
for research question 1, fitted both a Poisson model with number of games as offset and a binomial logistic model
compared the Poisson and binomial model fits using AIC and BIC
found the binomial distribution fit the data better than the Poisson distribution, ΔAIC = 3.35, ΔBIC = 3.35
adopted a mixed effects logistic regression approach for all subsequent analyses

spans.assertion: used the BOBYQA optimization method for parameter estimation in the final approach
found BOBYQA was four times faster and resolved the non-convergence issues from the initial approach
analyzed all 116,014 complete dyads in the final approach
compared random effect structures for referees (random slope for skin tone, nesting referees in home country, and a combination) against the initial crossed random-intercept baseline
found that nesting referees within their home countries without a random skin-tone slope produced the best fit, ΔAIC = 13.85, ΔBIC = 4.20, χ2[1, n=116,014] = 15.86, p < .001
compared more complex random effects for players (nesting in clubs, league countries, or clubs nested in league countries) against the new baseline
found that none of the more complex player random-effects structures improved model fit
specified a non-nested random intercept term for players in the final model
the final-approach analyses corroborated the results of the initial approach
found darker skin-toned players received more red cards than lighter skin-toned players, ORlightest,darkest = 1.382 [1.120, 1.705] (final approach)
the skin tone effect was again not moderated by explicit racial prejudice, OR = 1.220 [0.445, 3.345]
the skin tone effect was again not moderated by implicit racial prejudice, OR = 0.474 [0.001, 385.189]

spans.note: reports that Morey and Wagenmakers, in a separate analysis, found the skin tone effect contingent on seven outliers (0.3% of dyads)

spans.assertion: found that six of the seven outliers identified by Morey and Wagenmakers were already excluded from this analysis due to missing skin tone or position data
removed the remaining (seventh) outlier from the analysis
found removing the remaining outlier did not change the conclusions, ORlightest,darkest = 1.416 [1.149, 1.745]
